utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. The hearing is now resumed. Registrar, would you have the accused brought in? (Accused brought in).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear? I see the Prosecutor does. Is the Defence able to hear? Does Mr. Blaskic hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right then, we can resume the questioning of our last witness, who was not being covered by protective measures. I think he can be brought in and we can begin the examination, since we only did the preliminary part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President and your Honours, good morning counsel. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, I hear you fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, you are under oath as a Prosecution witness. Did you rest well? Do you feel good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine thank you. I got a good rest and everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon. FUAD ZECO (continued) Examined by MR. HARMON (continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, I beg your pardon, could I hear the interpretation a bit louder, please? Just a bit louder, please. That is fine. I think it is fine now. Do I hear you now? Fine, fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Zeco.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, when we concluded the first portion of your examination, you told us a little bit about yourself and your life in the Vitez municipality. Now let me ask you, Dr. Zeco, can you describe what life was like in the Vitez municipality before the start of the war, and particularly between the various ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Life in the territory of the municipality of Vitez, I can say in the area of the Lasva Valley too, because I was there throughout the Lasva Valley, life was very pleasant there. I usually say that it was even an idyllic life, because all the different peoples lived together there, and life was truly wonderful in the area of the Lasva Valley, namely the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there harmonious relations between the various ethnic groups, Dr. Zeco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. The interethnic relations I think were such that no distinctions were made between Croats, neighbours, Serbs, Muslims. I personally, who moved throughout the area, was welcomed everywhere. I had the strong feeling that I was welcomed as a very dear guest everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, Dr. Zeco, did relations between the Muslims and the Croats begin to change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after the elections in 1991 these relations were changed, in a way. Changes certainly did take place in relation to the previous system, the previous state system, which was only to be expected. However, as time went by, these relations became ever more complicated and complex, later on difficult, and finally they went through the worst thing possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO seize control of the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think that some time at the beginning of 1992, when the Serb Chetnik aggression was carried out against Bosnia-Herzegovina, namely in the immediate vicinity of the Lasva Valley, the relations were already disrupted, the relationship with the Serbs. The HDZ was already politically active, very active. Later on when the military option was there too, namely the HVO, then the situation was really complicated, and profound problems were there in the territory of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the HVO seized control in the Vitez municipality, did life for the Muslim people become more difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims who lived in the territory of the municipality of Vitez, particularly those who were in the field of communications and who knew what was going on, they were -- excuse me -- exposed to certain physical assaults even, by HVO members. They were attacked physically. Money was taken away from them, various objects were taken away from them, automobiles, they were not in control and that was the situation as concerns the members of the Muslim national group in the territory of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims in the Vitez municipality, as a result of what you have just described, form the Co-ordination Board for the Protection of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what I wish to speak about. In the area of Rijeka, where we lived together, the Croats and Muslims together, I was in touch with my neighbours, at least with some of these people who were prominent in this area of Rijeka, both Croats and Muslims, and I asked them that we meet together, which they accepted. These were prominent people, and we managed to meet at my place, at the veterinary station. There were 10 or 15 people present. Perhaps there were a bit more Croats than Muslims present. These people were intellectuals, and that is the question we raised; what was going on? What could we do? What should our attitude be in this situation? However, we did not have a special answer to all of this. At that point in time, it was the Croats who said they would see these friends of mine who were there, they said they would see, but at that point in time they could not say anything specific, but they were hoping that everything would be all right. However, nothing came out of it. The situation was getting worse and worse, and later an invitation followed, the Party of Democratic Action called upon the Muslim people, all prominent Muslims, people who were well respected in the territory of the municipality of Vitez were invited to come together to meet, and to see what could be done, regardless of their ideological orientation. This invitation was issued some time in mid 1992. I responded to that invitation, I did. The problems were presented there, the overall situation, and a civic body was set up on that occasion, which was supposed to have a certain task, a certain role. It was called the Co-ordinating Body for the Protection of the Muslim People. I was also elected to that body, and I became a member of this Co-ordinating Body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did you play, Dr. Zeco, in this Co-ordinating Body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I had specific tasks. Throughout my stay in the territory of the municipality of Vitez, as head of the veterinary service, from the very outset and throughout this period, I was a member of the municipal civilian defence staff. I was in charge of the development of livestock production, so I had certain -- had a certain role to play in the development of agriculture, so in the Co-ordinating Body I was in charge of resolving issues related to agriculture, to livestock production and problems related to civilian defence, so this was the specific role I had to play in the Co-ordinating Body for the Protection of the Muslim People.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of your role, being involved with agriculture, can you explain to the Trial Chamber some of the types of problems, the specific problems that you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could. Regardless of all these problems that cropped up, in the structures of government, in terms of the way certain institutions and services were to function, life went on nevertheless. In the area of the municipality of Vitez, namely the Lasva Valley, agriculture was the most important activity, so spring was coming up and all problems related to agriculture were supposed to be resolved and I was involved in all of this. There was already a certain division of power. It is well known that a Croatian government was set up there, of the HVO, namely the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. A Co-ordinating Body was set up for protecting the Muslims, which also tried to function and to make it possible for life to go on. Afterwards a War Presidency of the municipality of Vitez was established, but agricultural activities had to be pursued too. I was personally involved in all these different commissions, both in terms of the Co-ordinating Body and also by the HVO. They were supposed to set up joint commissions for the spring and autumn planting and sowing. This commission was supposed to work on a larger scale, within the Chamber of commerce, so I was involved in all these activities. The Co-ordinating Body and later the War Presidency gave me personally explicit instructions that I pay great attention to this, when seed is distributed, for instance, that Croats should not have any kind of disadvantage, that seeds should be distributed evenly and fairly, and in that situation, I think that all of us who were involved did our best and did things properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time while you were involved in the Co-ordinating Body, was a problem brought to your attention involving Muslim butchers and cattle? Could you explain what that problem was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I had a very difficult problem. In Vitez itself, and this was characteristic of the town of Vitez, there were 14 or 15 butchers who were running their own small businesses. Perhaps I could acquaint this distinguished court with the fact that Vitez was a transit area between the rural and urban areas, cities like Banja Luka and Sarajevo, so a lot of meat and meat products were going through Vitez. That is why it was a thriving business. There were 14 or 15 independent meat businesses. These butchers would buy livestock at Busovaca, Travnik, Bugojno and once they went to the market in Busovaca and all the cattle they bought at the market was taken away from them by the HVO, by HVO soldiers, namely the military police of the HVO. They came to see me, they expressed their regrets -- I was in charge of veterinary inspection too, and they asked me to help them with this problem, because they had purchased quite a bit of cattle then. I went to the municipality. At that time there was an HVO government there, I told them what it was all about and they said "we will solve that". I know that after a few days, in Busovaca there is a market always on Saturday, Saturday is the market day, so this was a few days later, and some of the butchers were asked to come and to get their cattle. They went there, but none of them got all their cattle back. Perhaps a few heads of cattle, the big cattle, is what they got, but they could not get their sheep or their lamb. That is what they did not manage to get back. So this is the role I played with regard to this question, and this activity of mine within the Co-ordinating Body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These butchers were Muslim butchers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The butchers who you were intervening on their behalf, were they Muslim butchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were Muslims. I must say that when I asked them, they told me that there were a few Croats, a few Croats too whose animals were taken away, and later taken on to the Kacuni military barracks. Later on, I found out that these Croats, that is what the Muslim butchers told me, had a much better deal and that some of them even earned a profit. That is what I know, and that is what I was told then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, where had the cattle that the Muslim butchers had purchased, where was that taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was taken to the army that was located in Kacuni. It was taken there and handed over to that army. I got that information from these butchers, because later they went to that area where the military barracks were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, Dr. Zeco, did you become a member of the War Presidency, and if so, can you just explain briefly what your role was in the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In January 1993, when it was established, I was appointed a member of the War Presidency as the commander of the civilian defence staff for the municipality of Vitez. I held that office until 10th October 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served in the JNA. Actually I was demobilised from the JNA in 1953. Immediately upon demobilisation, I went to university to study veterinary medicine. After that I graduated from university, I became a veterinarian and after that time, I was never involved in the military in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not a member of the Territorial Defence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Vitez, but I was a member of the municipal staff for civilian defence, civilian protection, and there were a few seminars, a few training courses, all in the domain of civilian protection, all the activities that are involved in the field of civilian protection, from radioactive, atomic, biological warfare, so I learned all about that. I attended these seminars at that time throughout Yugoslavia, even went to Belgrade, republican and local seminars, but my orientation was to be involved in those activities that could help people who needed help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now in your living in the Vitez municipality, did you get to know Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I often had the opportunity of meeting him. We did not have a very close relationship, but we would say hello to each other, exchange a few words. In certain situations, we even had discussions on certain matters. If this distinguished court wishes to hear about this, perhaps I could mention that he knew that I was involved in certain political activities, so he presented his views and brought up certain questions that we then discussed. There was a characteristic case. This was in the offices of the municipality. My wife worked there; she was involved in geometry and I would often meet Mr. Anto Valenta there because he often sought maps, so we started discussing these maps. He was looking for certain locations there, and he said that it was desirable to have Muslims in one area, Croats in the other and Serbs yet in another area. At one point, it seemed outlandish -- perhaps I am using too crude a term, but it really seemed outlandish and we discussed this, but he said that that should be done, but he would like to say that it should be done in a humane way. I did not understand that at all. What was this "humane way" of resettling people, making them move from an area in which they lived to an area where they do not want to live? So I had the opportunity of having such discussions and conversations with Anto Valenta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, did you have occasion to see the following people on television: Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, Tihomir Blaskic, Mr. Kostroman? Did you see those people on television in the Vitez municipality prior to 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of 1992 or rather 1991, 1992 and 1993, local television was organised by the HVO, or rather the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Community, later Herceg-Bosna, local radio and television. In Busovaca and in Kiseljak and in Vitez. On local Vitez television, they were present all the time. This was a local TV station. It only had Croats who were editors, Croats, so it was their media that made these broadcasts throughout the area. From 1992 until the fateful date of April 16th, this media campaign, as it were, was present throughout. As the Prosecutor said, you could see very often, all the time, Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, Dario Kordic Anto Valenta, Kostroman Ignjac and others too, but these people were on local TV very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was Tihomir Blaskic presented or introduced, or described, when he would appear on these television programmes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihomir Blaskic was in uniform. He was commander of, I think it was -- he was commander of the units in the Central Bosnia region. He always was wearing uniform, that is how he appeared on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn just briefly to Dario Kordic. What sorts of views was he expressing through the course of these television programmes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dario Kordic was exclusively a politician, and he obviously expressed political views, and he presented himself as a representative of the Croatian people. Very often, he attacked the official authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He very often would single out certain actions of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, President of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said that these leaders who represented the Muslim population were not doing things right, that they were not doing things well for all people and that the Muslim population would not fare well because of that; that they should ally themselves with the Croatian people, that they should submit to the Croatian authority and that that would be good for them. On several occasions he even expressed something like threats. I remember well a statement on local television that he gave when he said that should the Muslims not comply, that they would disappear from that region. Personally, I was dismayed by such a statement, because I knew and I was very friendly with the Kordic family, with his father, who is also a veterinarian, so a colleague of mine, and his mother, and we were very good friends. We even exchanged visits very frequently during the period of time when I worked in the Vitez area, I would substitute and I would step in and replace him when he would go on vacation. He was a veterinarian for the Busovaca municipality, so I would take over his job when he was on vacation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, do you remember approximately when Dario Kordic made the statement that the Muslims would disappear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this was some time in the second half -- maybe September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me turn your attention to Tihomir Blaskic. What types of subject matter would Tihomir Blaskic address? What kind of statements, as you recall, did he make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, as far as I can recall, also mentioned that the Croatian people need to become militarily capable, so that they would be prepared to defend themselves, to fight for their rights, even militarily, if needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make any other comments about Croatian aims or Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since this is purely military matters, I did not enter that much into that, but he did point out the need for arming for defence the military organisation. Those were mostly his statements. But since I was not very interested in things military, I did not pay that much attention to it, but basically, he called for the Croatian people to organise themselves so that they could demand their historical rights and if necessary should realise them even militarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of statements did Anto Valenta make on the television, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Mr. Anto Valenta even made threats to the Muslim people, and was also making comparisons, saying the Croat people were armed whereas the Muslim people were not. He said that they were -- they had their own army, that they were secure, and that they should be put under the command of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make any public statements, Dr. Zeco, about the inability of Muslims and Croats to live together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, on several occasions. He made such statements on several occasions, saying that it would be desirable to create areas for Muslims, for Serbs, for Croats, that that would be the best solution. That was the sense in which he made his statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, Mr. Kostroman. What kind of statements did he make, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Kostroman was making very similar statements to what Mr. Anto Valenta was stating. Those were the subject matters that he raised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often, if you can recall, did you see these four gentlemen you have just testified about appear on television? Was it once a week, was it more frequent or less frequent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very frequently. As I said, these television programmes were there daily. They very frequently appeared on television, very frequently, so you could comfortably say that in a single week, all these gentlemen would appear there at least once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, I would like to turn your attention to a man by the name of Darko Kraljevic. Do you know Darko Kraljevic and the Kraljevic family and if so, can you explain to the court how you knew the man and the family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Darko Kraljevic as a child, who grew up with my own children. I knew him very well from when he was very small until he grew up. I was very good friends with his family, because we were neighbours. His father was the director of the Forest Bureau. We lived in the immediate neighbourhood. We often would meet both officially, because we shared the field of forestry and agriculture, and Darko's mother was a colleague of my wife's, because they worked in the Land Registry office, and I often gave rides to Darko or his brother Slavan and mother, or I would take them to school together with my children, or their mother together with my wife, so that for years we were friends in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, if I could direct your attention and the witness's attention to exhibit 103. The court may wish to examine the exhibit at the same time the witness is. I am not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have exhibit 103? Is it a map of some sort? Has it already been identified?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, if you could turn your attention, please, to exhibit 103, I am going to come over next to you and ask you some questions about it. Dr. Zeco, could you please approach exhibit 103? Yesterday, Dr. Zeco, you showed us the location of the veterinarian station, and your home. Could you now show us, and point with the pointer, the apartment building where Darko Kraljevic lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kraljevic lived over here, where the arrow is showing. This was the building where Darko Kraljevic lived. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, I cannot hear a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are not getting an interpretation, you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am not getting translation from this system. I am getting the Bosnian Croat translation, not the English translation -- I think it is my fault, your Honour, I do not think I had it on the right number. Could you say something please, Dr. Zeco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just showed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I am sorry for the interruption. Please, Dr. Zeco, you pointed to number 3 as being the apartment building of Darko Kraljevic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he lived with his wife and a child that was born later and that is precisely the building where he lived, that is where the arrow is pointing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now point out to the court where the home of Darko Kraljevic's parents was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates). This number 4, the arrow is pointing precisely at the building which belonged to Darko Kraljevic's house, it is their own property. I know this because I was frequently in that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point out the forestry station and where that is in the Rijeka area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates). This is under number 1 and the arrow points directly to the forestry station building, where very often there were certain HVO units and military units, so they occupied that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, will you take a look at that once again. You indicated that it was number 1. Yesterday your testimony was number 1 was the veterinarian station. I would like you to examine closer and ask you where the forestry station was located, what number and what arrow points to the forestry station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was number 5, I apologise, so number 5 is the forestry station. Can you hear me? I do not know if I was heard on this. It was number 5, so I apologise, because it was actually number 5 and number 1 is the veterinary station. Am I being heard?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you are. Lastly, Dr. Zeco, can you point out on this particular exhibit the location of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Hotel Vitez is under number 6, and the arrow points directly at the building of the Hotel, the Hotel structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zeco. You can take your seat again. Dr. Zeco, was Darko Kraljevic a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I know the whole situation as it developed. Darko Kraljevic at first was a member of the HOS and wore the HOS insignia, at the beginning of his military career, if I can call it that way. Later on, I think that was in the middle of 1992, the HOS units were absorbed into the HVO units, and then he was a member of the HVO units, and they were known as the Black Knights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see Darko Kraljevic in an HVO uniform and can you explain to the court those occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I even remember a television programme which showed, in a rather decorous way, how the HVO units were being absorbed into the HVO. There was a line up and then there was a ceremony whereby they became the HVO units, and then later they became known under the name of the Black Knights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just looking at your transcript right here, Doctor, and the translation says that you saw: "... a television programme which showed, in a rather decorous way, how the HVO units were being absorbed into the HVO." Do you mean how the HOS units were being absorbed into the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the members of the HOS, of the HOS, then became the HVO units. That was the television programme that was broadcast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Black Knights also known as the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did Darko Kraljevic have in the Vitezovi, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the leader, he was the commander of this unit, and I frequently saw him. He always had an escort of several soldiers and entourage and I think they provided protection for him. I think that they behaved as subordinates to him, so they were something like his bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him wearing HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how often you would see him with an HVO uniform on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, the insignia on this uniform, it is a question I have about the translation here; "when was he wearing the insignia", and then I heard, "when was he wearing the uniform".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask another question, Mr. President. After the HOS units were absorbed into the HVO, did you see Darko Kraljevic in an HVO uniform with HVO insignia and if so, can you explain to the court when and where you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Darko Kraljevic was wearing a camouflage military uniform with the HVO insignia on it. You asked me whether I saw him frequently; I would meet him frequently and on one occasion, if I may say so, I had taken my car to be serviced, and I drove it to this work canal and at that point, Darko Kraljevic drove in in his car. This was a private shop. My car was immediately pulled out. We greeted each other, he just nodded his head, so my car was driven out and his car was put in. They took out a machine gun, several crates of bullets were pulled out, and he told me that he needed to go out to the field and there were the HVO insignia there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, I would like to focus your attention on another event. Can you explain to the court the incident when you were attacked in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I usually would spend most of my time out in the field, and I was coming back from Krizancevo Selo at that time and I was passing the school in Dubravica and HVO unit was stationed in that school building and after I passed, a car came up behind me with the HVO soldiers. This is a very narrow road. I could not pull over and they were driving behind me. It is about 100 metres away from the intersection where it feeds into the main road, so I sped up a little bit, but still cautiously enough so that I would not slide off the road, but they caught up with me and they started bumping me from behind and then I turned off and their vehicle passed me and came out on to the main road and about 50 metres later, they stopped, and three or four soldiers jumped out. There was one who pulled at the door of the passenger side, so I leaned over to open it, and then he grabbed -- he jumped in with his legs first and he hit me in the face, and I was bleeding, I realised that my nose had been broken. Then a soldier came out and pointed the automatic rifle and another soldier came and took him by the arms and said "okay, let him go" and he told me, "get going". I closed the door and I started in the direction of Vitez. I immediately, without thinking, went to the police. I came to the police station, I was all covered in blood, and at the door of the police station, the chief of the police station, Mirko Samija, was standing. I had very good relationship with him, he asked me what had happened, what was that, and I told him what it was, I told him that I was attacked by the HVO soldiers, and then he said, "okay, let us go", and he got into my car and we went to the health clinic. He ordered two policemen to immediately go to that spot where this incident had happened and to determine what had happened. So I went to this health clinic with him, to the health centre and I was given medical care there, and after that, I went home. When I arrived home, about half an hour later, the same chief of police station came to my house with the two policemen, and apologised. He said that at that time, they could not do anything, that this was the military, that there was nothing he could do, that it was too dangerous, but the time would come. Then he expressly told me to go to the Travnik hospital to have a proper exam and to bring him the finding of this, so that he could have the document with him. From the experience that I already had, I realised that he was powerless to do anything and that is where it all remained, the whole incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify one or two points, Dr. Zeco. Mirko Samija, the policeman to whom you reported, the incident where your nose was broken, was he an HVO civilian policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, could you repeat your question? I did not quite hear what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Dr. Zeco: to what organisation did Mirko Samija belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirko Samija was head of the police station. I know that personally, because when the representatives of the Muslim people and of the then established HVO government were trying to reach agreement on setting up joint authorities et cetera, I know this for sure, because I was one of the people who supported the appointment of Mirko Samija as head of the police station. I did this on behalf of this Co-ordinating Body for the Protection of the Muslim People. I wanted Mirko Samija to be appointed head of the police station, and he was head of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the HVO police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. To your knowledge, Dr. Zeco, were any arrests ever made of any HVO soldiers who had attacked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Doctor, were any HVO soldiers ever prosecuted for the attack on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, by all means no, because Mirko Samija told me that he was powerless, that he could not do anything, and that at that point in time, he would not do anything on his part, and he personally apologised to me because of that, but he said that that is the way things had to be at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am prepared to break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to take our break now and resume in 20 minutes at 11.35. (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.35 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing now. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can begin in now, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Dr. Zeco, one question on the last subject area that you covered. The gentleman by the name of Mirko Samija, was he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirko Samija was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, if I can, Dr. Zeco, to 16th April 1993. Where were you on the morning of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, I was at home. I had spent the night there, and on the morning of 16th April, at 5.30, we could hear explosions and shooting. Only my wife and I were at home. It came as quite a surprise to us. We jumped out of bed, and what followed was like a film. Everything was so fast. Everything happened so quickly. I got up at 5.30. At 6.30, I was already arrested, taken to the building of the veterinary station. In the morning, when we got up, I was still wearing my pyjamas. Soldiers came, in front of the house. They knocked at the door, my wife opened the door. Two soldiers walked in, they told me to get dressed. They were wearing full war gear. It was quite unusual, though, that their skin was all painted and black. I think it was like soot, and they told me to get ready and that they would take me away. Two soldiers walked into the house, but there were three or four of them, three or four soldiers around the building. I got ready, I got dressed, I saw that they were armed, and I went out. They took me to the veterinary station --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, Dr. Zeco, were these HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were HVO soldiers with HVO insignia on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask them where they were taking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I asked them "what is going on? Where are we going", and they told me that I would see. I saw that there was no specific answer that they were willing to give, and that all further discussion would be superfluous. I knew these soldiers, but I just let them do what they had to do. I did what they asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that they took you to the vet station. Did they leave your wife at your home, or did they take your wife with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my wife stayed at home. I wish to mention here, though, my wife's words. She said, "do not take Fuad, take me". They said that they did not have anything to do with her and that they had orders to take me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife stay at your home during the entire period of your captivity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she stayed at home all the time, because I was taken to the veterinary station. That is about 100 metres away. She had the opportunity of coming to the vet station when they allowed her to bring in food, so she stayed in our house while I was at the veterinary station. Later, when they moved me from the vet station to the school in Dubravica, she remained at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, you were taken to the vet station, can you explain what happened at the vet station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the vet station, we were met by a man I knew, in uniform, Zeljko Matkovic, who said that he was the one who decides over there, and that he is the person we were supposed to address. There were two or three other soldiers in HVO uniform too. I also knew them. When I was brought to the veterinary station, I found about 10 or 15, I do not know the exact number, other people at the veterinary station. They were in the hall, in the office, and in the examination room, the room where animals were examined. At that point, there were some 10- or 15-odd people, I cannot tell. Others were being brought in too. All of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all males?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people ultimately were detained at the vet station while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were counting how many of us there were, and I know that at one point we managed to count 76 men, 76 of us. 76 Muslims were detained in the veterinary station in the basement. The conditions there were very, very poor, because the basement was underground and during the winter, water could penetrate. Fortunately there was no water there then, but we had to sit on wood that we found there, so that we could protect ourselves from the dampness. Upstairs, there were two very small offices, and members of the HVO were there primarily, they were coming and going. There were a few of our detainees up there too. I had the privilege to stay in these offices and the rest were in the hallway and in the room for examining animals. All of it was very small, we were crowded, we spent three nights there, and on the fourth day, we left the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the range of ages of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the way it was. I think that from the area of Rijeka, all the men -- I cannot say 100 per cent, but most of the men from the age of 16 to 70 were detained there in the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, after you arrived at the veterinary station, was there any interrogation or questioning about weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the next day, the day after we were brought in. The man who supervised us, under whose control we were, this Zeljko Matkovic, he summoned us and told us that now all of us who had weapons and ammunition at our homes should say so then, and that HVO soldiers would come and take each and every one of us home in order to bring in these weapons. But he told us to pay attention, and he particularly pointed out that by no means should anyone have arms and not surrender them, because members of special units would be coming in, specially trained units from Herzegovina, and he said that they were capable of finding these weapons, even if someone tried to hide them, and that it was impossible to hide weapons, and that if that were done, they would burn these houses down and whoever would try to do that would bear the consequences. After that warning, some people said that that was the case, that they had weapons and then soldiers escorted them to their homes and they brought these weapons in. These were negligible quantities of weapons and ammunition. As far as I can remember, it was one rifle, a Karabin, there were some bombs, a few pistols and I think that there were two hunting guns as well. When it was all brought together, it was in a basket where people would usually keep their linen, it was a basket that big. Then one of them said "what is this? Are these all the weapons that the Muslims have", and that was the end of that. Again, he threatened us, he said that we should be very careful because the members of the special units who came in from Herzegovina specifically for that purpose were coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were detained at the veterinary station, what happened to your car, Dr. Zeco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had two cars. I owned both of them, because we used our own cars when we were on duty, but we were compensated for that, for using our own cars, and I had one car only for family use, and the other one, the Renault 4, was used only for my work. The next day, a HVO soldier came, and he asked me to give him my car keys, because he said that my wife -- is this okay, is this working? My wife said -- they first went to see my wife. They asked her to give them the key and she said she did not have the key, she said that I had the car key and that I was at the veterinary station. A soldier came and he asked me for the key to the car and I gave it to him, because I knew from the experience of others that their cars were taken away, so he took the keys and he went to the garage, which was only about 20 metres away from the building. He came back shortly and he said "I cannot turn it on". He asked me whether I knew what was wrong with my car and I said I did not know what was wrong, although I did know what was wrong, because I had disconnected a cable, because at that time during the night, people's cars would disappear, Muslims' cars, and this was a minimal precaution that I had taken. So they said, "all right", they pushed the car out and I looked through the window accidentally and I saw HVO soldiers driving my car. They realised why the car did not work before. The next day, they came to take the other car. I said that this time, and that was the truth, this car that I was using for work was really out of order, and that I could not agree with the repair man, he was supposed to come in one of those days to repair the car for me, so when I told him that the car was no good, that I could not use it and he threatened me and he said "we know you and you are going to pay for this". But they went to see the car and they realised that it was partly taken apart they gave up on taking that car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your release from custody many days later, and we will get to that later in your testimony, did the HVO ever return the car that they had taken from you? Did they ever return your car to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever compensate you for the car? Did they ever give you any money for the car they had taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, never. I never got any compensation or anything in relation to my car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, I would like to turn your attention to an event that occurred while you were in custody at the veterinary station, that is a large explosion that occurred and that you heard. Can you explain to the court what warnings, if any, you received from individuals who were guarding you about that particular explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Within the building, within the area where we were detained, we tried to adjust to the situation and to help each other. But at that point, the same person came in, this person who organised this prison of ours, Zeljko Matkovic, and he said "all of you, each and every one of you, should go to the basement and that is it. Something is going to happen now". He said that we had to go to the basement. We were curious, we were surprised, wondering what it was. It was not clear at all, but he specifically asked us to hurry and to go down to the basement. The staircase was narrow and those people who got downstairs had to make room for others, so we were not moving at the speed they wanted. Nevertheless, we all did manage to get down and we huddled in there. It might be a room 3 metres by 6 to 7 metres, and a few moments after we got down there, we felt an explosion, which was really strong. There had been explosions until then too, but none of them matched this one. It was long, it was strong, and to the best of our knowledge, it was pretty far away, but it was something big. We did not know what it was all about, but then we realised that that is what was supposed to happen. As we were getting out, this same person, Zeljko Matkovic, said "now it is over with the Muslims". Again, this was not clear to us. He said, "now it is over with the Muslims".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later find out the source of that explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. Later, we found out, when we were transferred to Dubravica and when our families came, our wives, our children, when they would come and bring us food, they told us that in Stari Vitez there was an explosion, that the HVO had loaded fuel on to a truck, that drivers were tied up and this truck with explosives was sent to Stari Vitez, and that quite a few people were killed from the explosion, quite a few were wounded, and also that there was a lot of material damage involved. Later on, we found out about all of this, about all the effects of this, so that was the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, you said you remained at the veterinary station for three nights and on the fourth day you left. During the time period when you and the other detainees were at the veterinarian station, I would like you to briefly describe whether men in captivity were taken out to go dig trenches and I would like you to summarise that, if you could, within just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the very first moment when we were detained, from time to time HVO soldiers would come to see Zeljko Matkovic, and they asked him for five, six, ten detainees that they were supposed to take away. Later on we found out that they were taken out to dig trenches. This happened throughout those three days, and perhaps the fourth day too, although I am not too sure. I think we were taken away at 12.00, but people -- prisoners were taken every day to dig trenches, and we knew where they went, because we were curious, we wanted to know what was going on, what the situation was and we knew that they were taking them to the area of Rijeka to dig these trenches, trenches along the lines, and there were some war operations going on over there already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the detainees who had been taken to dig trenches killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately there were people who were killed, there were people who were wounded. According to what the people who went there told us, some were killed by bullets coming from rifles and they did not know from what side, a bullet would simply kill a person, whereas Ibrakovic Jusuf was killed by a member of the HVO who took them out there to the line where they were supposed to dig trenches. That is where Hurem was killed, his name was Hurem. I knew him very well because he was a neighbour of mine over there too. I know him, he had a horse, and he would take his horse and carriage and carry goods that way and that is what he lived on. He had four children. He supported them. His horse was in very poor health, so I had to intervene often. He was killed too. As far as I can remember, Salko Salibasic was also wounded. Also after the end of the war, as I was carrying out my duties, I did my best to ensure medical treatment for him in the hospital in Tuzla. He underwent five or six operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco -- do you have something else you would like to add to your testimony, before I ask the next question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were also some other people who were wounded there, and then they were transported to the hospital. There were some who were lightly wounded too, but they never came back. Later, I learned that they were taken to another prisoner camp which was in Vitez, up in Vitez, very near the clinic. That is where they were given some medical care and so that is where they stayed. They never came back down there, where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day did you leave the veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were detained on the 16th, so three nights and the fourth day was 20th April, when we were transferred. We were told to get ready, and to line up to go to the forestry station, which was very close from there, about 100 metres, that we would be transferred to another place. We still did not know where that was going to be, so we walked in file and then they said that this was enough. We came to the forestry station, to the courtyard there and there was a minibus there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken, Dr. Zeco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the school in Dubravica. Later, after our group was transferred there, the rest of them who had stayed in the vet station were also transferred there, so we were all reassembled there, and this was in the school building in Dubravica near the railway station. In Vitez it was locally known as the area around the railway station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in captivity there until 30th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were detained at the Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived there, we found another group, a sizeable group there. There were men and there were also some women and children. We found out that these were some families, so those were wives and children of some of the men. There were no men though, they were all from Ahmici. There were other ones who were detained from Santici, Novaci, Krizancevo Selo, railway station. In other words -- Sivrino Selo, so the surrounding areas, and since immediately next to that there was the wood-processing factory, and they had night shifts, so the men who were coming out of the night shift, so there were men from other outlying areas, so these were the workers there who had worked there, so they also were detained in the school in Dubravica. Further, there were some refugees from other municipalities, who, following the Serb Chetnik aggression and the JNA aggression, had been put up in Vitez from Jajce, from Mrkonjic, so in sort they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you arrived at the Dubravica school, did you hear any small arms fire, any gunfire in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we arrived in Dubravica, during that night, there was shooting around, all around in the area. In my assessment, it was sporadic and sometimes it was closer by, sometimes it was farther away, so we knew there was fighting going on between the army and the HVO and depending on the war, the combat situation, that is how the shooting was occurring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the shooting was going on, did the detainees -- did you hear any particular threats uttered by the HVO in respect of what would happen to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were hoping, we counted on the luck turning in towards the BH army, that we would be liberated, and at one point, the shooting came very close, we noticed that, and we could also observe it by the behaviour of the HVO soldiers who were there with us in the school, because they came and told us expressly not to leave the school by any means, because everything around it was mined, so we would all be killed. They said "do not rejoice, do not rejoice about your army".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Please continue. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue, Dr. Zeco.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Do not rejoice", because as they said, "even if the army came, it is not going to be good for you, because down there, we have a fuel truck filled with fuel and we would blow it up so you will not fare well", so immediately we started enquiring among each other and indeed we learned from some who had seen it that there was a fuel tank or a fuel truck there which had fuel, because it was used for heating of the school, and since I had this role for -- I was involved in the civilian protection, I started immediately thinking what we could do if something like this took place, what we were to do. Somehow we started planning if this should happen that we would break some of the bars that were there and we assigned this operation to some people, so that we would -- if such a thing could come that we would keep a certain order there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Zeco. In the translation there appears to be a reference to a "fuel truck" or a "fuel tank". Was what was described to you by the HVO a fuel truck or a fuel cistern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like a cistern, like a reservoir. It was a tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the record has been clarified. So without going into great detail about essentially the escape plan should something happen, would you continue with a description then of the events that happened after these particular threats were made to you and to the other detainees. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. However, at one point when this shooting really drew close, we observed -- we sensed at one point that we were by ourselves, that the soldiers who used to guard us there had gone, had disappeared, so at one point, the shooting stopped and the soldiers reappeared. Then we learned that the army had advanced and that the soldiers had retreated. However, the shooting suddenly stopped and the soldiers reappeared, we were there surprised, we were disappointed, because the army did not appear, we were not liberated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later learn why the army, the Armija, had stopped its advance in the direction of the Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They had threatened us that should Armija come, that they would blow up the entire school building with that fuel that they had there. Then we found out later, when we were expelled, I had got in touch with command of the army and I asked them at that point why did they stop there, why did not liberate us then and then they told me, those officers, that they had received confirmation from the HVO that if they continued to advance towards the school building that they would blow up the Muslims who were detained in it. This is what the BH army officers told us, this is the information that they gave us, and they cited it as the reason for their not liberating us. This was later verified by the command as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, do you remember the approximate date when this advance stopped, that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on the 22nd, 22nd April, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus your attention on a different subject, and that is trench digging done by the detainees from the Dubravica school. First of all, can you explain to the court what you saw while you were there, in respect of that particular subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one of the big problems that we had during our stay in the school in Dubravica was precisely the demands by the HVO soldiers to give as many prisoners as possible to go to dig trenches. The soldiers would come in, they would come together with guards who were guarding us, and then it was their choice, they would choose 10 to 15 prisoners. Mostly they were picking people who looked physically more fit, so a group would leave and then the next group would come in and take another group of prisoners with them, and so it would happen that within one hour three separate groups were being taken to dig trenches, and after a while, they would come back. There were situations that those who came back -- because these demands for prisoners were more and more frequent, so it would happen that if a group came back, they would be turned around and taken to dig trenches again. There were those who looked physically fit but in fact were sick, so it was very hard on them. Then there were some who managed not to go, so we realised that things were not right here, and so we started talking among ourselves how to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, before you get into this area of your testimony, let me ask you, approximately how many times a day would the HVO come to take civilian detainees and approximately what percentage of the men who were detained were taken out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that I cannot be very far off if I say that at least a third of the total number, which included the old and women, so a third would have been involved and taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever taken to dig trenches, Dr. Zeco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was never taken to dig trenches. I did not go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You started to describe what you and the other detainees saw as a problem developing. Can you explain very briefly what the problem was and what you and others did to solve the particular problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. That was a problem. We saw that certain prisoners were finding themselves in a very difficult situation, because they were completely exhausted, and they risked being taken there to dig trenches again, so we made an agreement and we established a delegation of sorts. I was part of it and Pasa Mujanovic was part of it, and Mirhat Hodzic, who used to be a mayor of Vitez before he was replaced by Ivica Santic, so the three of us were representatives of the prison Muslims and we asked to see the camp commander, Marinko Placic, to address him with respect to this problem, to explain the situation, that there were people who were not able to dig trenches and were taken there, and we had a very specific proposal for him. So we presented that problem and that proposal to him, and we said that we would put together a list of people who could go to dig trenches, and that the people who were coming and asking for a certain number of people to go and dig trenches, that we would provide a list and that we would sort of arrange for them, so that we would not have situations where somebody would be overexposed to this and others would not, so we put together a list of all people up to 50 years of age, taking into account their health condition, and so we selected a group. During this time that we were there, Pasa Mujanovic was in charge of this, so in case this demand was passed on to us, he would be the one who would decide if he would assign people, and so if the HVO soldiers came in and said, "We need ten", these people would just respond themselves. This proposal was accepted by the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever object to the use of civilians being used to go out and dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we first went there, we told him that the situation was very difficult, that people had a lot of problems, that there were people who were at the end of their strength, that he should not be doing that, that there were sick people there, et cetera, but he said "this is a job that has to be done", because he received an order that he had to secure prisoners to go and dig trenches, and that there is no discussion possible there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, please. I was turning to my colleague. I did not quite understand the interpretation, whether the camp commander accepted that suggestion or did not accept that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, did the camp commander, after you made your proposal, did he accept your proposal or did he reject your proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he accepted the proposal. This was solving the problem of involvement of prisoners in trench digging, but there was the order, it had to be done, that the prisoners had to be taken to dig trenches and it was -- but it was up to us who would select the people, but we had to obey the order, that is when the demands came, we had to provide enough prisoners, so the order had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, Dr. Zeco, that that is then how prisoners were selected to go dig trenches after they were -- after demands were made by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I apologise, I did not understand the question. Would you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The system that you recommended to the commander was then followed for the remaining days while you and the others were in captivity, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, after prisoners had returned from the trenches where they had been taken to dig, did you have conversations with them about their experiences, where they had been, what had happened to them? You can answer that with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, did they tell you where they had been taken to dig trenches? Can you identify the various locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken -- I am going to go from one end of the municipality. These were the border areas. This was the area where the combat operations were taking place, so this was the area of Kuber, Nadioci, Pirici, area of Sivrino Selo, Krizancevo Selo, Tolovici, Krcevine, Gornja Dubravica. For the most part that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Rijeka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, if I could have the photograph turned over, I would now like to have the witness's attention directed to exhibit 29I, which is the large map. Dr. Zeco, if you could kindly approach the map and mark with a -- there should be a bright pink pen in front of you -- could you mark the areas with that bright pink pen -- Dr. Zeco, in front of you there is a -- that is correct. Could you mark those areas with the bright pink pen where prisoners had been taken to dig trenches, starting with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the area of Nadioci, here it is, Nadioci. This is the area of Kuber, here it is, Kuber. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, could you please put a mark, at least a longer broader mark in the areas you are referring to, because this is going to be used as an exhibit and we have to see what you are marking. Would you identify by name each of the areas that you are marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the area of Kuber; this is the border area with the municipalities of Busovaca and Zenica, so these are the territories of the other municipalities, Loncari, and then this area that goes to the north, due north towards Zenica and then Vrhovine, so these are the areas. These are the farthest points of the Vitez municipality. This is the area where they went to dig trenches. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Kuber. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you specifically, in your direct examination you testified that the prisoners told you they went to the area of Nadioci. Have you marked that area on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the area of Nadioci. It is right here, there it is. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, you next mentioned the area of Kuber. Have you put a mark in the area of Kuber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here is Kuber. This is the area of Kuber. This is north of Nadioci. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned the area of Pirici. Could you put a mark in the area of Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pirici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the area of Krizancevo Selo. Could you put a mark in the area of Krizancevo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map). Here is where Krizancevo Selo should be. Hold on. That is that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the area of Krcevine. Could you put a mark in the area of Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krcevine is this area. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Sivrino Selo. Could you mark that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Gornja Dubravica? Could you put a mark in that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gornja Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the area of Tolovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tolovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And lastly you mentioned the area of Rijeka. Could you put a mark in the area of Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zeco. You can sit down now. Dr. Zeco, those are at least the areas where the prisoners told you they had been taken to dig trenches. That does not necessarily represent the exact locations of the trenches themselves, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move that Prosecutor's exhibit 29I be admitted into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, that can be admitted as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I could have placed on the ELMO exhibit 29C. Dr. Zeco, would you take the pointer, please, and with that pointer, would you please indicate the locations of the following areas. Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For your information, Doctor, the centre of the first circle is the Hotel Vitez. Can you tell me, at least looking at that exhibit, how many kilometres away from the Hotel Vitez Nadioci is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six to seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I have that focused a little bit better? Thank you very much. All right, Doctor, now the area of Kuber which you also mentioned in your testimony. Where is that? Could you put the pointer on Kuber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many kilometres is that from the Hotel Vitez, according to that exhibit 29C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you place the pointer next on Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many kilometres is Pirici from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next could you put the pointer on Krizancevo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sivrino Selo. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three kilometres, Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the area of Krizancevo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area of Tolovici, how far away is that from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates). Four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next could you place the pointer on Gornja Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is that from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, could you place the pointer on Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to that exhibit, how far away is Rijeka from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you very much, Doctor. Mr. Usher, I am finished with that exhibit, thank you kindly. Dr. Zeco, now let me turn your attention to -- actually, let me ask you one more question in respect of the trench diggers. Were trench diggers from the Dubravica school killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people who were killed and people who were wounded. I am not sure, but I do know for sure that some people were killed and that some people were wounded. The wounded did not come to the school, they were probably taken away for medical treatment immediately. I do not know what they did with the killed people, but I do know that some people were killed and that other people were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, let me turn to another subject and that is your release from custody at the Dubravica school. Can you explain what happened, how you were released and the circumstances of your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received information from the people who were guarding us that we would be released, but before that we were supposed to say whether any one of us wanted to leave Vitez; if so, buses would be organised to take us to Zenica, so that those who wished to go could go, whereas those who wished to stay at their homes could say so, could say that they wished to go home. But before that, we were all supposed to go to the offices that were prepared, there were two or three tables there with people who were keeping records. There were some women there too who were keeping these records, who had these lists that were already made, and before that, we were supposed to say for the record what we wished to do, to declare whether we wished to leave or whether we wished to stay. We were told to line up and to go, two by two, to one of the tables. One group was supposed to go to one of the table, the other group was supposed to go to the other table and that is what we did. I personally said that I would go home, and I should particularly like to point out here that all the young people who were sent out to dig trenches, which was obvious, each and every one of them, regardless of the commitments they had, the remaining families they had at their homes, they all said invariably that they would go to Zenica, while the older people said, as I did, that they would go to their homes, and that is what was done that day. We were told that buses would come there to take us either to Zenica or to Rijeka, and those who were in the immediate vicinity of Dubravica, that is Novaci, Krizancevo Selo, Stanice, they could go on foot by themselves, whereas the people who lived in Rijeka and Vitez could wait for the bus if they so wished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, were people who were being released given a free choice to go either back home or to the area outside of Vitez? Were there any suggestions made as to which choice should be taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I was cautioned by a HVO soldier. He told me personally, "it would be better for you, Doctor, to leave Vitez". I knew him, and I understood that this was a friendly caution, and that it was in my interests, but I said, "no, I am going home".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, did you ultimately arrive at your home on 30th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was waiting for other people, because we wanted to move in larger groups and I thought it would be best to take the bus after all, so I was waiting for the bus there on the side and there were HVO soldiers there and they had beer, crates of beer, they were there right next to us, they were already tipsy --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, excuse me just a minute. Let me move past that, because I want to move this testimony along a bit. Let me ask you, after you arrived home, did anything occur at your home the first night you were at home, or did that night pass peacefully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night passed peacefully. I came home, and there were no problems that night. I spent that night at home. My neighbours came, Muslims, women, Muslim women. Men did not come, because some of the detained men did not come that evening from Dubravica, and I said that we were all released and I said that we were given a choice and that we could wait for the bus, and probably there were special reasons involved, but at any rate, I know the next day that each and every one of them had left this camp which was at the Dubravica school, so that evening, nothing special happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Zeco, I am going to conclude my examination at this point, and we will pick it up again with what occurred to you on the second day. Mr. President, if this is an appropriate time, we are going to go into another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, this would be the proper time. I would however remind you about what was said during the status conference, which I do not want to repeat before this witness, but you know what I am alluding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Specifically in terms of your own list, Mr. Harmon. I thank the witness and I appreciate his patience and calmness in answering these long questions which remind him of events which are very painful, but I do permit myself to remind you of your own commitments, Mr. Harmon, and if they cannot be honoured then the Trial Chamber must take other arrangements.
