utterances.text: Yes. I know of other cases too. I do not know of a single case when the perpetrators involved in any incident were held responsible or bore the consequences that they were supposed to bear. I am not familiar with a single such case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same line, you mentioned that Darko Kraljevic, when he was drunk, he became fearful and brutalised the people, and you even added that other military HVO were in the habit of getting drunk. Was this almost a frequent event, that they get drunk and brutalise the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second half of 1992, as time went by, as the fateful conflict of April 16th was getting closer, it became increasingly undesirable for Muslims to be near the members of HVO units, because one never knew how one would fare and what kind of situation one could get into. I personally had really been moving around a lot, and I was provoked a lot, I was insulted and I tried to avoid meeting them, especially in the later stage when units from other parts came to the municipality of Vitez, those that did not include soldiers from the Vitez municipality area, but from other territories, because they did not know me personally, they did not know the other local people either, so the local Muslims avoided getting in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In short, as a conclusion, would you consider that, considering this accident of the attack against you and the other features of brutality, do you think that the HVO were under no strict discipline and they could act with impunity towards the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that these soldiers were undisciplined. One could feel that they had a military discipline, but at any rate, there was a certain kind of discipline that they had as far as Muslims were concerned. I had the opportunity of being in the company of Croats too, but these HVO members, soldiers who did not know us, they would react and they would make me feel unwanted, but they had a military discipline, and as regards their attitude towards the Muslims, I think that they were not prevented from doing certain things that they did. That is the impression that one got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that when the detainees were given the choice after their return, they were given the choice either to leave or to stay in Vitez. What happened to those who decided to stay in Vitez? Do you have any knowledge or experience of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. All of those who stayed on after being released from prison, all of those who stayed on, except those in the urban part of Vitez, they all left the municipality of Vitez, except 90 or 100 people. Those were the Muslims that remained in the urban part of Vitez, so all the Muslims had left. They either left of their own volition or they were expelled, so only 90 to 100 people were left. I am not sure, but I think 96 have stayed on, 96 Muslims have stayed on only in Vitez, after the Muslims were expelled from the Vitez municipality in the area where the HVO was operating after the conflict with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, what was the percentage of the Muslims who stayed afterwards compared to the percentage in the beginning, if you know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell, because this is the urban area, but approximately from my own point of view I could say that it could only be up to 5 per cent of the Muslims in the urban part of Vitez. When I say the urban area, I am including Rijeka too, Mlakici also, the part towards Kruscica, the part towards Gacice. Out of the total number, it is possible that the percentage was not larger, I think it was not even 5 per cent, that it was less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it before the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the very centre of the town, the Muslims and the Croats and the Serbs, according to the census from 1991, they were about 40 per cent out of the total population in that area, because the centre of Vitez had a mixed population. The members of all three ethnic groups lived there, and they were equally represented, approximately, but I think about 40 to 50 per cent in the centre of the town were Muslims, in the central part of the town of Vitez. Those are my estimates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question concerns the warning you had concerning the explosion in Stari Vitez. You said that they told you the day before that, I think, "you have to go to protect yourself", and you discovered the next day that there was a great explosion as a result of the truck which exploded in Stari Vitez. Who warned you about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were warned that something would happen. The organiser and the person who led the detained Muslims in the vet station, he was the one who informed us of this, and he asked all of us to go to the basement, because he said that something would happen. At that time, we could not have known, we had no information as to what would happen. We went there, we were guessing, we were talking about all of it and after about an hour, we heard a strong explosion, an explosion that was strong, and we were wondering what had happened. It was unusual compared to the other detonations that we heard that day and everything. After a short period of time, this same person came and said, loud and clear, "now it is over with the Muslims". During the day, as our families came, we found out that it was an explosion, that it was a truck bomb that had exploded that was in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that, thank you. I just wanted to know then that there was a preplanning of the whole thing and the leader of the detainees knew about it, knew that there was a planning and a scheme to explode Stari Vitez; is that the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, that is exactly it, because he knew that this was going on, those soldiers that were present there sort of rejoiced, looked happy that this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Doctor, you spoke about finding refuge for yourself and wife with the brother of Ivica Santic, who later lost his life. Did other Muslims also find refuge with other Croat families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to apologise here if I somehow mentioned this brother of Ivica Santic, Zvonko Santic -- he was not killed, but he really sincerely helped me. There were other Croats, a sizeable number of Croats who really helped the Muslims. However, it is also a fact that there were some Muslims who asked Croats for help, and they would openly state that they would gladly help, but they did not dare do it, and I know of several examples personally of Croats who did help the Muslims, and I know that they suffered very grave consequences on the part of these military units, those Croats who helped. In some ways, I think they may have even suffered worse things and more brutal consequences than the Muslims themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you yourself still have Croat friends in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a number of Croat friends in Vitez, and it is my hope that we are still friends. There were Croats who did try to help me in that period, but they let me know that they could not do it, and I had friends, and the friends that I had were not the ones that I selected on ethnic grounds, they were all good people, and they were my friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go to these television broadcasts in which General Blaskic participated. We do not have the actual words which he might have used, we have your impressions of what he said. Was it your impression that the position which he took when he spoke of military matters only was that his conception of his task was to use the military apparatus under his command to implement the policies of the HVO, whatever they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression, precisely, as regards the statement by Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, that he was a soldier, a soldier that serves, that he is committed to the ideals and that he has a model of the professional expertise and I think that he very professionally discharged his duties. His statements were such that he as commander would ask and demand that everything is prepared and enabled to carry out the task that it is supposed to carry out and to reach the goal which was set out in all of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That goal to which you refer would have, on the basis of his statements, been set out by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That goal was set out by the policy, the policy that existed, because a significant part of all this was the involvement of the entire leadership, which even included the Republic of Croatia in Vitez; for instance when the authority was, the local government was suspended, and when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established and when the police station and the municipal buildings were taken over, it was the flag of the Croatian state that was flown there, so that everything that was going on in the territory of Vitez came from the higher places and not within the local area which would be this municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, forgive me for interrupting you, but I am only asking you of your own impression as to what he understood to be the source from which the goal would come? Who would set the goal for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not assess or say if anyone specifically gave him this task, but the fact is that everything boiled down to invoking the right of the Croatian people, and it was in that context that his appearances on TV came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go to those appearances on TV. You know sometimes you could have on TV a panel discussion in which each member of the panel speaks individually. Then you could have another kind of show in which a group of people appear to present a common programme. You said you saw General Blaskic on several occasions, together with a group of people on TV. Was the position this, that each member of the group was speaking separately and only for himself, or was the position this, that each member was presenting an aspect of the group's common policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. These were not discussions really, but in fact certain positions were expounded, positions that were clear, and its goal was to present a position that was part of that policy in this given situation, so these were not discussions during the appearances of these leaders, be they civilian or military. So they were presenting the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A last question concerns Mr. Kraljevic and the HOS. I think you said that at one point the HOS came to be incorporated within the HVO. Do you remember that branch of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HOS become incorporated in the HVO before 15th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a TV broadcast, and it was shown that the HVO -- that the HOS was incorporated into the HVO and that was I think in the latter half of 1992. That is when they joined the units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One little supplementary question to that last one. After the HOS became incorporated as part of the HVO, did members of the HOS wear any insignia or other identification marks connecting them with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did. They also had certain other insignia, but for the most part most of the members had the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Doctor, I have only one question, you must be already very tired and the Tribunal does understand your position. You were kind of a privileged witness, and I hope that you understand what I mean by "privileged". I know that you did suffer, but at the same time you were a prominent person and someone who was trusted by Croats and by Muslims as well, this is what I wanted to tell you. You who were a witness to all those events, I wanted to ask you a question: do you have a feeling that that level of sufferance, level of destruction and the level of hatred, whether it was the result or the cause, could have been attenuated, alleviated by the military or politicians within the framework of historical factors and political considerations that you told about to Judge Riad? By admitting the Croatian revendications, do you think, by looking back in the field, that the level of sufferance by the population could have been lowered down somehow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the most precise answer to your question would be by citing an example, and with your permission, that is how I would answer this question. In Mali Mosunj, which is an exclusively Croatian community, two pigs were taken ill, they were infected. I came over there and I gave them injections and so I gave them therapy and told this woman that I would come back tomorrow, because they may need additional treatment. The next day, when I came back, both pigs -- both ran high temperature and were refusing food and were completely exhausted. Now they were completely -- they were very lively now, they were vivacious and I was met by this woman and she was very joyous and she said "thank you, Doctor" and then she added "you see, Doctor, they are telling us to be against you. How can I be against you and you are doing such good things to us?" Then my answer to her was that all this, whatever was being done there was being directed, was being said to be done by certain persons who told them that this should be done this way, and that it was my -- I felt honoured, and also I feel very honoured now that I have been given an opportunity to give my own contribution, as far as I could, to your mission and I wish you all the best in this mission of healing so that this would not happen to the future generations, the things that happened to all three ethnic groups in that area, the Muslims, the Croats and the Serbs, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. This testimony is now finished and it is also the end of our hearing today. The Tribunal is thankful for your coming here, for your testimony, and we wish you all the best for the continuation. I would kindly ask the usher to escort our witness. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will continue on Monday at 2.30, so Monday at 2.30, because the courtroom will be taken up by someone else. (5.40 pm) (Court adjourned until 2.30 pm on Monday, 29th September 1997)
